bib.title: Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agent Plasticity: Measuring Self-Improvement Through Experience". Harman Singh (UC Berkeley and Meta Superintelligence Labs), Anton Bakhtin, Rulin Shao (Meta and U. Washington), Gabriel Synnaeve, Ilia Kulikov, Rob Fergus, Sanjeev Arora (Princeton), Kurt Keutzer (Berkeley), Jason Weston, Anuj Mahajan, Anirudh Goyal (last two joint supervisors; Meta). Preprint, arXiv:2610.08902v1 [cs.AI], 6 Oct 2026. No venue.

COVERAGE: All 43 pages extracted, 130,218 chars; I read the text of every page. The references (about chars 38-56k) were skimmed. The appendix prompts (I.3 to the end), most appendix figure panels, and the per-game figure data were skimmed or are not extractable (plots). I read none of the plotted values; numbers below come from text only. I read the target note (lines 1-335 of 533; the remainder, past the "Efficiency metrics" table, I did not read).

TARGET NOTE FIT: 06-evaluating-agents.md is about grading one agent's outcome/trajectory/components and repeat runs (pass@k, pass^k). It has no section on evaluating agents that learn over time. This paper measures self-improvement across checkpoints. The nearest hook is "Non-determinism: run every task k times" (a one-line bridge: score at checkpoint 0 vs later, held-out split), or "Efficiency metrics" ("cost per success", which is cost-normalized and the closest relative of Psat). I did not see lines 336-533, so check whether a "long-horizon / memory / learning" section exists there. It fits no other note in the folder better: 03-eval-datasets (held-out splits) and 09-reading-results (curves vs endpoints) are secondary. My recommendation is a short new subsection in 06, "Agents that improve: score the learning curve", or a sharpens-style citation if the note already covers the cost metrics. The paper makes no claim about grading single-run agents.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Claim: Endpoint capability and acquisition efficiency diverge. Claude Fable 5 reaches the highest fitted performance, but GPT-5.6 Sol has the largest plasticity.
 number: Psat 298 (GPT-5.6 Sol), 233 (Claude Opus 5), 57 (Fable 5), 14 (Opus 4.8) pp per $1,000; GPT-5.6 Luna 0 (no reliable rise); GPT-5.5 not established.
 setup: Held-out in-distribution (ID) score, mean over chess (Hard and Easy), Go (5x5) and Hex (6x6), frozen weights, 20 checkpoints; cost in USD at provider prices; 90%-of-rise saturation fit.
 quote: "GPT-5.6 Sol has the highest estimatedPsat at 298 percentage points per $1,000 of mean per-game learning cost, followed by Claude Opus 5 at 233, Claude Fable 5 at 57, and Claude Opus 4.8 at 14; GPT-5.6 Luna shows no reliable rise under the specified criterion and is assigned Psat = 0."
 where: Section 3.4, p.7
2. Claim: Self-improvement under an identical interface is model- and task-dependent. Some models gain a lot, some stay flat, and some decline.
 number: Hard chess held-out ID, checkpoint 0 to the 16-20 mean: Fable 5 37.5% to 73.3%, Opus 5 25.0% to 66.4%. GPT-5.6 Sol starts near 0% and reaches 36.9%. Opus 4.8 reaches 19.0% in Easy chess only (from 0%).
 setup: Hard chess: 16 training, 12 held-out ID, 12 held-out OOD games per checkpoint vs Stockfish 16 at 20k nodes. Score = 100(W+0.5D)/N. Unfinished games count as losses.
 quote: "in Hard chess, their held-out ID scores rise from 37.5% and 25.0% at checkpoint 0 to 73.3% and 66.4% averaged over checkpoints 16–20."
 where: Section 3.2, p.6
3. Claim: Gains do not carry across games, and OOD transfer is weaker.
 number: Go: Fable 5 ID 20% to 80%, OOD 0% to 50% (checkpoint 0 to 20). Hex: Sol ID 40% to 77.5%, OOD 28.1% to 78.1%. Opus 4.8 loses ground in Go but improves in Hex. Opus 5 improves in Go, then drops sharply at the last checkpoint after a tool-making error.
 setup: As above. OOD means stronger opponents, not new tasks.
 quote: "Claude Opus 4.8 loses ground in Go while improving substantially in Hex."
 where: Section 3.3, p.7
4. Claim: In NetHack, only one of six models shows a reliable gain.
 number: Opus 5.5 mean score about 2k (checkpoints 0-2) to about 6k (36-40); saturation at checkpoint 11; Psat 61.75 normalized points per $1,000. Learning cost $1,072.73 up to saturation. Other five models: "n.s." (Sol declines ~570 to 420; Luna ~210 to 120).
 setup: 10 fresh seeded Valkyrie games per checkpoint, checkpoints 0-40, 2,460 games, one lineage per model, native Claude Code and Codex harnesses. Scores rescaled with anchors 213.6 = 0 and 6,526.98 = 100.
 quote: "Its fit to checkpoints 0–40 reaches saturation at checkpoint 11, withPsat = 61.75normalized score points per $1,000."
 where: Section 3.3 p.7; Appendix C p.21
5. Claim: Low artifact reuse accompanies weak improvement. High reuse still leaves most failures happening while an artifact is in use.
 number: Share of relevant decisions without artifact use (Hard and Easy chess pooled): Luna about 98%, Gemini 3.1 Pro about 87%, Opus 4.6 about 51%, GPT-5.5 about 28%, versus 2-6% for Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and Sol. The strong improvers have about 0.16 identified failures per relevant decision against 0.38 for the rest; 83-99% of their remaining failures occur with an artifact in use.
 setup: Gemini 3.1 Pro labels offline, six-stage pipeline (Table 4), checkpoints 1-20 pooled. About 98% of chess moves after checkpoint 0 count as "relevant".
 quote: "most of their remaining failures (83–99%) happen while a relevant artifact is in use"
 where: Section 3.5, p.8
6. Claim: Local diagnostics can move without task performance moving.
 number: Opus 4.8 in Go: successful-reuse share rises from 59-65% to 93% while held-out ID falls from 40% to 10-25%. Opus 4.6: failures-despite-use rise from 6.5% to 52% while failures per relevant decision stay flat (0.42 to 0.41). GPT-5.5: reuse 96-100% at checkpoints 2-8, then 32-50% from checkpoint 9, with artifacts unchanged.
 setup: As in claim 5.
 quote: "Reuse, failure composition, and task performance therefore capture distinct aspects of persistent learning."
 where: Section 3.5, p.9
7. Claim (qualitative): Notes and rules pile up without being followed. GPT-5.5's opening book returns 6.Nxe5 before its own guard runs. GPT-5.6 Luna's notes tell it to play the first legal move (0.65 of held-out moves at checkpoint 20, below 0.2 before) because it was running out of its 64 calls per game.
 where: Figures 18-19, pp.~26-27

METRIC DEFINITIONS (verbatim)
- "We operationalizeagent plasticityas held-out performance gain per unit learning cost." Eq. 3: P_score = (S_T - S_0) / C_T, in points per $1,000; can be negative; declines after plateau.
- Eq. 4: fitted curve S_hat(C) = S0 + A*C^h/(C^h + C50^h), four parameters fitted jointly by binomial maximum likelihood.
- Psat = (S_hat(C*) - S0)/C*, where C* is the first observed checkpoint at which the fit reaches 90% of its rise. If the fitted rise is under 10 pp, Psat = 0. If saturation is not seen within 3x the final cost, report "plasticity to date".
- Learning cost includes rejected reflection attempts; Eq. 2 sums training-phase and reflection-phase calls. Priced in dollars as "the closest available proxy"; "This measures learning cost, not physical computation."
- Failure taxonomy: F_absent (no covering artifact), F_missed (covering artifact unused), F_used (artifact used, failure remained).

LIMITS
Stated:
- "Plasticity is therefore a property of an agent under a particular learning protocol rather than an intrinsic scalar property of the underlying model."
- Efficiency depends on provider pricing, saturation-fit assumptions and extrapolation.
- Diagnostics are observational, not causal. Artifact use does not show effectiveness, and failure after use does not separate bad artifacts from bad application.
- The design does not separate environment feedback from the extra compute spent on reflection. Budget-matched reflection without feedback is proposed as future work.
- Separate lineages do not show that artifacts transfer across tasks.
- Held-out sets are finite, so checkpoint-level noise is real.
- NetHack: changes across checkpoints "mix learning with game difficulty". Opus 5.5's three best games give 69% of its checkpoint-10 total. It scored 2.6-25x the others at checkpoint 0. The other lineages used earlier harness versions.
Unstated or my reading:
- One lineage per model per game, as far as the text says. The paper states "Each model has one lineage" for NetHack and does not mention repeated lineages or seeds elsewhere. Psat rankings therefore rest on a single trajectory. I found no variance, CIs or p-values in the text beyond "parametric bootstrap" intervals (not given numerically) and one p = 8.23e-7 for Opus 5.5's NetHack fit.
- The failure/reuse labels come from one LLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro). No agreement with humans or with a second judge is reported. The only checks I found are in the prompts (verification stages).
- The models are anonymous or unreleased (Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna). Models have different harnesses, with a gateway fallback for non-Fable models in Go and Hex.
- Easy and Hard chess, Go and Hex are averaged "equally" for Figure 1. Not all models are in all games.
- The reflection feedback differs by game: strong in chess (a skill-20 Stockfish gives centipawn loss per move), lighter in Go and Hex, none in NetHack. Plasticity is therefore not comparable across games.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES / CHECKS
- Psat units: Figure 1 says "pp per $1,000"; Section 3.4 says "percentage points per $1,000 of mean per-game learning cost". NetHack Psat is in rescaled "normalized score points". The 61.75 NetHack number is not comparable to the 298 board-game number.
- The abstract says "the agent that ultimately performs best need not be the one that improves most efficiently". The evidence is one pair (Fable 5 vs Sol), and Sol's chess endpoint (36.9%) is far below Fable 5's (73.3%).
- Sol is the most plastic on board games, but declines in NetHack (570 to 420).
- Figure 6 caption: the artifact-conditioned success rate "can be high even when artifacts are rarely used".
- Section 3.2 says Opus 4.8 improves "modestly and mainly in Easy"; Section 3.4 says Sol "surpasses" Opus 4.8 "in both plasticity and eventual performance", yet Sol's Hard chess ID is 36.9%, so that comparison seems to rely on the combined three-game curve. I could not check it from the plots.
- The 19-cell reuse/gain correlation is stated without a coefficient.
- The "Fable 5" and "Opus 5.5" naming varies between "Claude Fable 5" in text and "Fable 5" in figures. Minor.

BUILDS ON
Reflection, memory, skills: Shinn et al. 2023 (Reflexion), Zhao et al. 2024 (ExpeL), Wang et al. 2024 (Voyager), Wang et al. 2025 (Agent Workflow Memory), Liu et al. 2025 (Contextual Experience Replay), Didolkar et al. 2024 and 2025. Agent evolution: Hu et al. 2025 (ADAS), Yin et al. 2025, Zhang et al. 2026a,b, Lin et al. 2026 (MUSE-Autoskill), Wang et al. 2026b; Zweiger et al. 2025 (weight updates). Plasticity and continual learning: Dohare et al. 2024, Nikishin et al. 2022, Lyle et al. 2023, Lopez-Paz and Ranzato 2017, Chaudhry et al. 2019 (A-GEM). Learning benchmarks: Dou et al. 2025 (EvaLearn), He et al. 2026 (EvoTest), Asawa et al. 2026 (CL-Bench), Shu et al. 2026 (AgentCL), Harrington et al. 2026. Long context: Hsieh et al. 2024 (RULER), Liu et al. 2024 (Lost in the middle). Prompt/harness optimization: DSPy (Khattab 2024), GEPA (Agrawal 2026), Meta-Harness (Lee 2026). Environments: NetHack Learning Environment (Kuttler et al. 2020).

CODE
None general-purpose. Equation snippets only (Eq. 3-5, p.4-5). The artifact examples (Figures 12-19, pp.24-29) show model-written code, e.g. a chess `_AVOID.update(...)` exact-position guard and a draw-value ramp (`dsc = 150/400/900` at plies 220/240/280). Not worth keeping for the course.

FIGURES (candidates)
- Figure 1 (p.1): "Frontier agents differ widely in how efficiently experience helps them self-improve." Left: held-out ID score vs cumulative learning cost (log USD), with saturation points. Right: Psat bars (57, 233, 298, 14). This is the best single figure, since it shows endpoint vs efficiency crossing.
- Figure 2 (p.2): protocol diagram (act, reflect, held-out evaluation, artifacts: tools, skills, memory).
- Figure 4 (p.4): stacked bars of reuse and failure composition (absent / unused / used-still-failed). Good for the "where it breaks" idea.
- Figure 3 (p.3): checkpoint curves on train, ID and OOD for 8 models in Hard chess.
- Figure 5 (p.6): NetHack curves.
Extraction cannot reproduce the plots. The captions came from the text only; I did not run the figures script, so check the images before reuse.

PROBLEMS
- Plot values are not extractable, so any figure number not in the text is unverified.
- The text extraction splits words ("Weintroduceagent plasticity"). Quotes were cleaned of nothing but I kept the spacing glitches exactly as extracted. Fix spacing if you quote.
- No embedded instructions in the PDF text. The appendix prompts (I.1 onward) are agent prompts for the experiments, not directed at the reader, and I ignored them as data.
- The models named (Claude Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna) are not ones I can verify. The paper is dated after my knowledge, so I treat every figure as the paper's claim only.
- Fit to your repo rules: no human validation of the Gemini judge and one lineage per model, so mark confidence as low-to-medium if cited. Never cite the board-game Psat ranking as universal.
